Clarke Wright Performance Benchmarks

Source: vignettes/clarke_wright_performance.Rmd
clarke_wright_performance.Rmd

This article is part of the documentation of the R package, and the benchmarks were measured through it. The results also apply to the Python package, since it uses the same C++ solver.

In this vignette we discuss performance benchmarks of the Clarke-Wright algorithm implemented in this package by comparing the Clarke-Wright solutions of a set of problem instances with their best known value, and by measuring the run time on those instances.

The problem instance data

The problem instances we are basing our measurements on are provided courtesy of CVRPLIB and can be divided into eight groups1 of different characteristics:

  • Augerat A, 1995 (27 instances)

  • Augerat B, 1995 (23 instances)

  • Christofides and Eilon, 1969 (13 instances)

  • Fisher, 1994 (3 instances)

  • Rochat and Taillard, 1995 (12 instances)

  • Uchoa et al., 2017 (100 generated instances with 100 to 1000 sites)

  • Loggi, DIMACS 2021 (6 instances with 400 to 1000 sites, extracted from real problems)

  • ORTEC, DIMACS 2021 (6 instances with 241 to 700 sites, derived from real problems)

The data provides the problem instance as well as the best known solution, whose cost is available as the field best_known_cost of each instance. CVRPLIB lists the best known solutions of all instances of the first five groups as proven optimal, but only for 61 of the 100 instances by Uchoa et al. and for none of the Loggi and ORTEC instances. For those, a better solution than the best known one might exist.

The data of the first five groups is bundled with this package. The results for all groups are precomputed, so that building this vignette does not require downloading anything. See data-raw/perf.R in the package source for how they are obtained.

Relation to best known and trivial solution

The idea of this indicator is to measure where the Clarke-Wright solution sits in between the best known solution and the trivial solution2. Let γ\gamma be the cost of the Clarke-Wright solution, ω\omega the cost of the best known solution, and α\alpha the cost of the trivial solution. The measure ξ\xi is defined to be ξ:=1−γ−ωα−ω.\xi := 1 - \frac{\gamma - \omega}{\alpha - \omega}\,. The measure can move between zero and 1. It is zero if the solution is the trivial solution, and it is one if the solution is the best known solution.

Evaluating this for CVRPLIB sample data yields the following graph.

The mean value over all problem instances is ξ¯=98.9%\overline{\xi}=98.9\%.

Relative deviation from best known solution

We can also simply measure the relative deviation of the Clarke-Wright cost to the best known cost, ρ:=γ−ωγ,\rho := \frac{\gamma - \omega}{\gamma}\,, which measures how much savings we miss by using the Clarke-Wright solution instead of the best known solution.

The mean value over all problem instances is ρ¯=5.3%\overline{\rho}=5.3\%, i.e. on average, we miss out on around 5.3%5.3\% savings taking the Clarke-Wright solution compared to the best known one. For the instances derived from real problems (Loggi and ORTEC) it amounts to 5.8%5.8\%.

The slowest of the instances with 1000 sites takes around 5555 ms.
